projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Frederick B. Wolfe was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Frederick B. Wolfe. Mr. Wolfe served in the U.S. Army with the 90th Division. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was T5. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Wolfe's home in Willowick, Ohio, on December 6, 2004. Fred was 85 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: In 1941 I was living in Cleveland with my parents. Wasn't married then. And I was caught up in the draft.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Twenty -- 21.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were working, I assume, you were out of school and everything?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yes, I was working for Cleveland Pneumatic Tool Company at the time and had been with them about a year before the draft caught up with me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you drafted before or after the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before the attack?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Before the attack, yes. I was in Camp Shelby, Mississippi. And the day of the Pearl Harbor attack, I was having dinner with friends in Jackson, Mississippi. We were on a weekend pass from Camp Shelby. And I was a truckdriver and we drove a convoy up to Jackson, Mississippi. And we were really touring Jackson, Mississippi, in a car when the news came over the radio about Pearl Harbor. And of course, we were immediately all called back to camp, over the radio and any way they could get to us, get back to camp immediately. In fact, that was when some of the draftees that were in for a year had already been discharged and gone home, and they were immediately called back and set their suitcases down in the company street and said, "We're here." But -- and then from there we were in Camp Shelby.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many months had you been in then before December --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Just almost a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You had almost been in for a full year before the attack?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: I had almost been in for a full year and hadn't made plans to come home yet because I wasn't discharged. And I was -- I had gone in on February 7, I think it was, the year before that. So I was not quite complete a year. And from Camp Shelby, we left and were split up. Our battalion was split up, our company was split up. And one battalion went to Aruba for shore patrol or protection of the oil refineries and the tin smelters down there, and then we were sent to Texas City, Texas. And I was there almost a year before the war started. And then I was shipped from there to, what was it, Camp Kilmer?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Probably. In New Jersey I think it was?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: In New Jersey. In New York, New Jersey, yeah. Camp Kilmer I think it was. And from there we were shipped overseas. I joined the 90th Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember, before you went overseas, do you remember anything unusual or interesting that happened during your time training?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah, he married his wife.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, yeah, I got married.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's interesting.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: I got married. And we were down in Texas City to run shore patrol from -- well, our unit, with the broken-up battalions, the First Battalion was in New Orleans at Pontchartrain Beach, and we were at Texas City, and we were given the job of patrolling the coast there, Galveston Island and down to as far as Corpus Christi on the Texas coast.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: You might tell him that there were three oil refineries, a chemical plant, the only tin smelter in the western hemisphere --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: There were three oil refineries and the only tin smelter.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: -- a Navy base, an Army base, and an Air Force base there. That's what you were needed for.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: And Ellington field was at Houston and we had a, just kind of a makeup base at Texas City. And we were the Second and Third Battalions at Texas City. And then, oh, we did any one of several things, patrolled the beaches, and for a while I was changed over to Galveston and we moved ammunition out of the shore batteries onto railroad cars. And then we were at Fort -- what was the name of the fort there at Texas -- San Jacinto?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: No, San Jacinto was across from Bolivar Park, you're talking --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, that's where we were at, at Fort San Jacinto was the permanent army shore battery. And we spent, oh, we spent almost a year there, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the big fear U-boat attacks, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yes, it was -- and there was, while we were there, a submarine running loose in the gulf there. We heard about it. And we didn't see it. They had a running battle out in the gulf. And I see here, not too long ago, maybe you saw it in the paper, where when they were running telephone cable to Cuba, they ran across a sunken submarine off the mouth of the Mississippi River, off New Orleans. I don't know whether there was ever any effort to bring it up or not, but they made -- I saw it in the paper, where they had run across it while they were running telephone cable to Cuba. And I don't know what number it was or anything. I know they had an article about it in the paper. And we didn't see anything of it. But we saw some horrible, shot-up vessels come into the shipyard there at Galveston, while we were stationed at Fort San Jacinto, because we were right on the canal, and Bolivar Point was across the canal from us. But some of the merchant ships that had been traveling the East Coast would come in there and they had the whole sides blown out of them. And some of them there, you wonder how they were still afloat. But -- and then those were -- we'd moved from Camp Shelby to Texas, which Texas at least you got bed good. And Camp Shelby was a horrible place, a red mud camp I remember it. And of course, I went through the, what was it, the 1941 maneuvers that they had through the South.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that like in Louisiana or something like that?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Louisiana, Mississippi, yeah, through the boondocks and through the swamps. And of course, that was all before the war started and --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Fred, what about that boat from the German submarine that started to come ashore and you guys --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, we didn't see anything come ashore. But they ran across it. I was just telling him, they ran across it running telephone cable out in the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, the sunken U-boat, yeah.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah. I don't know what number it was or anything, but they told about it in the paper. And I thought how strange, maybe that was something we saw and that was the submarine, who knows. We don't know, because, of course, the Texas coast. In those days the whole length of Galveston Island was total blackout. And you didn't drive with headlights on the cars, or you drove with parking lights or blackout lights. And we, of course, went through a couple of hurricanes on Galveston Island where we couldn't get off the island for almost a week because the backwaters would come in behind the island and covered the highway and everything, we couldn't get back to the mainland at all. And our main camp was at Texas City. And then we had contingents in New Orleans and also down at Corpus Christi. And we never toured down that far. We mostly contended our -- our touring was mostly the Galveston Island and the shoreline there, but we never went to Corpus Christi though. And from there, we were shipped out of there to, where was it, it was a very small train out of Texas City directly up to, what was it, Camp Kilmer? It was a jumping-off point for going overseas and that's where I joined the 90th Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So had you been assigned to an outfit before that?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, I was with the, what was once the 166th Infantry, 37th Division. And that was broken up at the beginning of the war and we were sent on, oh, what do I want to call it, special assignment and split up, the battalions were split up, and I was with the, what's the Second and Third Battalion in Texas City, and the First Battalion was in -- the First Battalion, had they gone to New Orleans? I forget now. And then the other -- then maybe they were sent on to Aruba. And we were sent on to Camp Kilmer in New York and joined with the 90th Infantry Division. And I was a truck driver. And I was a truckdriver in the 90th Infantry Division carrying a, pulling a 57-millimeter antitank gun, which I was with through the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of truck were you driving?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: A low silhouette 6 by 6 Dodge. And of course, when we went to New York, they loaded us all on a British troop transport, the Evangeline was the name of her, it was a big British troop transport that sailed us over the North Atlantic in convoy to Liverpool.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that crossing okay, any problems on that crossing?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: We had a few alarms, submarine alarms, but we never saw anything. And as far as I know, we never got fired at. But we were in convoy. And I'll tell you that rough Atlantic can get rough, oh, it can get rough. You can be alongside one ship one minute, the next minute you're on top of the wave or down on the trough and that ship has disappeared. And the next minute you're up on top and you see that ship that was next to you. But no, I don't recall any sub alarms that we ran into all the way across. And we actually got into Liverpool without any action that I can remember or didn't see anything or hear anything. The sirens might have gone off, but we were in, I don't know how many ships were in the convoy. And we got up at -- we got into Liverpool and we went to a place called, I think it was Leominster, England, which was an army camp. And we stayed there, I don't think we were there a month maybe, maybe a little more, when we were shipped over to, shipped to -- where in New York? Port of New York. Boarded the ship called the Evangeline. And we shipped over and landed in Liverpool several weeks later, because we zigzagged all over the North Atlantic getting over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that crossing?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, it was in the -- gees.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In relation to D-Day, was it about what, six months before maybe?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, it had to be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So late '43 probably, right?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: It was before, it was before, well before D-Day. We were over there in time for D-Day, I'll tell you. And then they put us on a Liberty ship and shipped us across the channel. And it was on a day almost like today, gray and dull, drizzly, rainy. And I never saw a more desolate looking shoreline in my life. And I never saw so many ships in one place in my life as I did there. Men -- we went over on a Liberty ship and they off-loaded us onto a barge, gun and truck both. And they had a tug and the captain that was -- the Navy personnel that was on that barge and tug had made several landings before. And as we left the side of the ship, what shore batteries there were left that were operating on the French coast were firing at us. And this, when one shell would land, why this Navy captain, he would run the barge right into where that shell had landed and the next one would go right over us. So we got ashore without getting hit. But we had spent, in England, we had spent months waterproofing those truck engines so they would run underwater. And when we lowered the ramp to the barge to let us off, we rolled into water. I was sitting in that truck, I was up to here in water driving the truck. And if those engines were not waterproofed right, they weren't going to run. They'd stall like right now. Well, fortunately, I guess I'd done a pretty good job on mine because it kept running and got us ashore. But like I say, we were running water up to here on my waist sitting in the driver's seat. And so we got ashore in fine shape. But we went ashore at -- I think it was -- it was the southernmost beach. It wasn't the beach the rangers were on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So maybe Utah Beach?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Utah I think it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And June 6 was when you landed, right?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any idea, remember what wave that would have been?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: We were not in the first wave. We were not in the first wave. We were probably in the second or third, because we landed on day-plus-one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: So we were not on the initial landings. But the beaches behind this beach were full of canals. And we were told of us, that you only had one way to go, that the whole back beach was nothing but canals. And you had to go across one road. And once you got ashore, you wouldn't stop. In fact, we had a lecture from General Patton just before we went over. And of course, you probably are well aware of General Patton's language, he didn't spare none. And he said once you get ashore, he says you're not going to stop. You're going to keep going. Because if you stop, you're going to get the hell blown out of you. He says they're going to zero in on you and they're going to blow the hell out of you. That's exactly the way he put it. And he was right. Although he was rough and tough, he was a general that knew what he was talking about. And although he didn't like the, as he called them, waffle-assed generals in Washington, he'd pound the hell out of them, and he didn't care about his language, whether there was nurses or whatever there was in the crowds, he said it like he thought. And he was right, he was right, exactly right. And we didn't stop. When we did stop, we did get the hell blown out of us. And later on in Germany we had stopped in a town square. And while we were stopped there, they laid a shell right between the truck and the gun while the guys were trying to unloosen the gun from the truck, and they caught the whole gun crew. We lost them all from that. But that was while we were up still in the middle of the war, up in one of the German towns, and I can't tell you the name of them, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about the D-Day invasion, the time you were in Normandy?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, we went into -- got on the beaches and got inland, where we stopped initially. And those were the days when the Germans had what they called the screaming meemies, and that was the first thing we heard was wee-wee-wee-wee. And those were designed to explode on the ground and spread out, they'd cut your legs off. And they were weird sounding things. And of course, being greenies, greenhorns, going in, you had the hell scared out of you. Anybody that wasn't scared, don't say they were scared, is crazy. Because I'll tell you, they're something to be scared about. And we got ashore and, of course, the Germans had planted the fields behind the beaches with telephone size telephone poles, right close together, so the gliders couldn't land. They had to crash to land. They'd crash right into them. And I think the first thing I saw when we drove up one of the roads into the back beaches was a GI cut to shreds with his guts all spilled out in the ditch. Pretty unsettling, but, hey, that was the way it was. And paratroopers hanging from the trees. And I don't know what this guy had been hit with, a tank shell or what, but he was cut in two. He was cut in two. And we just progressed on up into the inland and the people -- and we were told, before we ever landed, not to trust the Normans, because the people on the Normandy peninsula did not like us. And they were right, they did not like us. And to treat them -- not trust them. And we got in and we worked our way down the Normandy peninsula. And every one of those houses on the peninsula had huge, huge wooden barrels of cider, apple cider. They were big things, as tall as this room, wooden barrels. And later on as we progressed through France and as we were coming into some of the towns, people would line the street like there was a parade and they'd have big pitchers of apple cider. And later, as we got in towards France, it wasn't apple cider that was in those pitchers, it was cognac. And the troops would come marching up the road and they'd pour these glasses of cognac out, and I mean they were something else again. But, in fact, one outpost we were on, a little French lady come out one morning, early in the morning, wanted to know if we wanted a picker-up. And yeah, it would be pretty good. Well, over there they didn't have coffee, they had -- oh, what's the other coffee substitute?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ersatz coffee, or what do they call that?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, I can't think of it. I know it as well as my name. Bitter stuff, terrible stuff. Anyway, she come out with a potful and a bottle of cognac. Got to have a kicker-up, and she'd pour the cognac into it. And of course, you know, what cognac tastes like. And so -- oh, I can't think of the name of the brew. I'll think of it maybe. But we worked our way on down the coast down to the Basse peninsula, Avranches. And as we went through Avranches, we went through the town of Avranches, and there were still snipers sniping at us. And they had the MPs out directing traffic as we went through the town to rush us along so we didn't get shot at. But they were cornering snipers up in the buildings that were sniping at us. And you just wondered as you went through there whether you were going to get shot before you got through. But -- and then that was -- let's see, that was well before the Battle of the Bulge. And then we got down into Saarbrucken, when that happened, and we were in Saarbrucken when we got word of the paratroopers being dropped. And that was in the wintertime, colder than hell, 20 below weather. And of course, as we'd stop, we would never -- with the gun and everything, we'd get the gun placed, and then we'd find a place, a house or something, and we'd make people move in another part of the house and we'd move in, so we'd get out of the cold. But it was bitter, bitter cold. And of course, the day the Bulge broke, we got word of the paratroopers being dropped and we got the hell out of Saarbrucken and backtracked. And I think it was somewhere in that space of time I wound up in the hospital with pneumonia -- or jaundice, yellow jaundice. Because I remember the doctor saying, looking at me and saying, "Hey, you're yellow." "What?" He said, "You've got yellow jaundice." And your skin turned all light yellow and you were just sick all over, I'll tell you. And then we were, was it after that, I guess we had encircled the German Seventh Army. And at Falaise Gap, we closed that gap. And I'll never forget that morning. All of a sudden the Germans made an attack on us and we were right in their way and it was like a shooting gallery in that place. And that was where I got hit with a grenade, caught me in the -- fellow next to me I understand was killed. I don't know who he was. You never did know who you were next to. And they had thrown a grenade and apparently he caught it and I didn't. I hit the ground and got it in the back of the leg. And with that -- have you ever looked down a German tank with about eight foot soldiers behind it? I did. Looked out of a cornfield and here was this damn tank just turning the corner of the cornfield. And I ducked back into the cornfield, and ducked, and it was -- I was wearing a raincoat, I know, and I hit the ground and just pulled the raincoat over my head. And I could hear these guys walking by me. They didn't know I was alive. They thought I was dead, I think. But I expected to get a bayonet in the back. And it never happened. And after everything quieted down, I looked down and they were gone. And here they were running right into a field hospital. And I don't know where they went to because the hospital never saw them. And I could feel my leg, because it was numbing up on me, it wasn't -- I just got a nick, fortunately I didn't get a bad hit. And of course, I had gotten right close to this field hospital. And I went back there and said, "Hey, did you see that tank?" And they didn't even see the tank. So I don't know where it went. Never saw it. But I know it had about eight foot soldiers supporting it. And I wasn't about to stand up and start shooting at it, because I'd have gotten killed real quick. But -- and that was the only wound I sustained during the whole war. I'll tell you, I had two angels riding on my shoulder.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that when you were wounded, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, I can't remember the dates, because they're 60 years away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. I'm just trying to get some idea.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: It was when they closed the Falaise Gap and trapped the German army. And the whole German Army, Seventh Army, surrendered at that point and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was that -- that was into the Battle of the Bulge, right? Or was that?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: That was before the Battle of the Bulge. That was before. We were still in --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still in France.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: We were still in France when that happened, yeah. And when the Battle of the Bulge broke, we were -- were we in Germany then? I know we were along the Saarbrucken River.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That sounds right.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: And we got word that paratroopers had been dropped. And it was this cold snowy morning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you laid up with your wound then? How long were you out --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: I wasn't laid up. It was a superficial thing that they patched it up at the field hospital and no problem other than my leg was awfully sore. It just caught me along the back of this leg. And nothing, nothing deep. It was shrapnel from the grenade. Somebody had hollered "Grenade," and I hit the ground. And I don't know, whoever was next to me got, apparently got the full blast of the thing and was killed, was what I heard later. But other than that, I fortunately was fortunate enough not to get hit again, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what else do you remember about the Battle of the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, I know I never saw the army move so fast in all my life when they got word that the paratroopers had been dropped. And we backed off and came back up into it. And I saw the vehicles that had been trapped. And that was the only time I saw General Patton up looking over his beat-up vehicles and troops. He was in his lead Jeep, and you couldn't miss him with that polished helmet and two pearl-handled revolvers. But he was looking over his troops. He was up there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember him saying anything or shouting anything?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, I wasn't that close. I wasn't that close to him. I just remember him in that lead Jeep just looking over his troops. And that's the first time I ever -- last I ever saw of him. And then, of course, later he was killed in France in a car accident. But he was a rough, tough son of a gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the guys like him, do you think, the guys in your outfit?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No. I don't think anybody really liked him, because he was a rough-and-tough general and he told you like it was. But his tactics, if they'd have let him go, he'd have been in Berlin before the war was ever over. He'd have shut Berlin down in a hurry. And they stopped him, because he ran out of fuel and -- he just was a rough, tough general. And I don't know, there was that incident he slapped that soldier. I don't know the ins and outs of that because I wasn't that close to it, but there was a big hullabaloo made about that. And, of course, he could have cared less. He could have cared less. And then we got into, oh, what was the name of the town we were in in Germany after the war. It was an ex-German tank arsenal where they had these little one-man training tanks. And of course, GIs get anything mechanical and they'd get it running and run the hell out of it. And they ran the drive shafts out of those things before very long. After we got on this base, and it was a military tank base is what it was, and, oh, gees, I can't even remember the name of it now, but we were just outside of Weiden, and Weiden was where the 90th Division headquarters was at. And oh, I had the name on the tip of my tongue before you came and I can't remember that. That was 60 years ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I'm sure we can find it in the 90th Division history book.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Probably, probably. And then, of course, we stayed there and that's where I started home from was there and came across Europe again. And I got into Czechoslovakia, that's where we met up with the Russians --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: -- at the end of the war. Happy. Happy. The Russian soldiers were, oh, they were all over us. We saw this column coming down the road, we were in -- I don't even remember the town.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Czechoslovakia?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: In Czechoslovakia.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That wouldn't be Pilsen, would it?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, I was in Pilsen. A friend of mine was stationed in Pilsen, and he came up and picked me up in a Jeep and I went down to Pilsen where he was stationed. No, it was not Pilsen. But we saw this column coming down the road and here it was the Russians. And they met up with us and, man, everything was happy go-lory, you know, and it was great. But it didn't take long before they told us on our way back home, on the camps that we were in, that we're on the Russian border, not to stray away from the camp into the Russian border, because if they picked us up, the American army would not know where we were at or how long it would take them to find us to get us back home again. But to stay out of their areas, because they were belligerent as hell after that and not nice at all. And of course, it was not long after that that the Russians and the Americans were not necessarily that friendly anymore. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any big celebrations on V-E Day when the war in Europe ended?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No. We just knew that it was over when -- and what was it the -- oh, when they bombed, what was it, when they bombed Nagasaki in Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah, that was a little later in August.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: That was a little later. And that ended the whole thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in Europe right on through that, then, through the atomic bombings?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, I came back home through Camp Lucky Strike.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Later than that?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, what do I want to call it? It was a discharge camp where they released us from Europe. And I don't even remember what ship we came back on. I think we came back on a Victory ship. But we were right -- Camp Lucky Strike was at LeHavre, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Right on the coast. And there were areas there we were told not to stray toward the seacoast because they were all mined. The mines were still in the ground and you're liable to blow yourself up. And so we were told to stay out of those areas, and which we did, and which we did. But it seems such a long time before we'd ever get processed to come home. Boy, that camp, I mean it was a big tent camp was what it was, a huge place. And of course, some of those -- well, in part -- some of the roads that we went on -- did you ever run across a 500-pound live bomb right in the middle of the road? You couldn't go any other way but over the top of it. And it's an American bomb that it was a dud. And it was buried in the ground, right in the middle of the road, and the only one way to go was over the top of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And would you actually, would you have to drive over it?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, right over the top of it. And I'll tell you, you went with your tongue in your throat. And then a funny thing, and this is unusual, we stopped at a place in Germany, at a farm, momentarily when the convoy stopped. And I couldn't speak German, of course, understood very little of it. But got to talking to this farmer, German farmer, and somehow or other it came around to I was telling him about Cleveland. And he said, "You from Cleveland?" I said, "Yep." He said, "I used to have a furniture at 65th and St. Clair." And he knew Cleveland like I did. It was so unusual. And a lot of people got over there, got stuck and couldn't get back. And we had a Jewish fellow that had left Germany, and he was with our outfit, an officer. And after the war, we were going to have a party on the base. And he grabbed me and he said, "You want to go for a trip?" I said, "Yeah." So we took my truck and we toured Germany. And he knew all the places where to get good wine. And I forget where it was, Wurzburg, we went, and he found a winery and he knew all the people and he knew where to go, and we got a big barrel of wine to bring back for the party. And they had quite a party that time. And he got, along with that, he got some 17-year-old Spanish liquor somewhere, I don't know where he got it, but, boy, was it good, knock you on your tail though. And every one of the filling stations, if you'd call them that over there, had basements underneath them. And the GIs would make for those basements. And what they were were wine cellars. And you'd get gown in those wine cellars and there was cascades of wine on either side of the hallways, going down through it, in racks. And by the time they got through that, they wouldn't hardly get back up the ladders. And then we got into Frankfurt and we stayed there overnight. And we had a lieutenant, Lieutenant Lockhart was his name, he was quite a boozer. Real good guy though. So he asked us if we'd like to go and see the champagne factory. Nothing left on top. There was nothing. Completely leveled. So we went down inside of it, and that thing went 12 stories beneath the ground. And when you got down there, I think this is where they started the bottles of champagne when they made it, and then every so often they'd bring it up a level as it cured. And when it got to the top, it was good champagne. So we went through it and we all got a bottle of champagne. And that night I was on guard at the headquarters and I see this guy weaving up the sidewalk and here was the lieutenant. And he come up to me and said, "Me and our trucks with the guns on, out front" and he said, "don't let anybody get into those trucks." I said, "No, that's what I'm here for, to guard the entrance." So the next morning we went out, pulled the tarps back off the trucks, and I don't know how he did it, but here he had gotten back into the champagne factory and here we had the backs of the trucks all loaded up with boxes of champagne, cases of it, goblets and all. And every once in a while we'd stop for a champagne break along the way. Those were some of the more comical things, I guess, that we'd run into. And of course, the Battle of the Bulge was a miserable, cold mess. And that was terrible. And then I had made friends with a little dog. I know the guys were so mad at me, because that dog just tagged me around, and they said, "Get rid of him because you'll give away our place if we're in anyplace where we have to be hidden." And he finally wandered off, I don't know where he went to. But that was a cold, miserable time, ice and snow. And it gets cold up there. In one of the -- when we were in the Ardennes, I had occasion to -- we went down into what apparently was a mining facility, real nice place, where we were able to take showers, water was still running and everything. We stopped there and we were able to get into showers and clean up and feel halfway decent after a while. And it was as we were coming out of that place, as we're going up into the Ardennes, we went by the cemeteries from World War I. And I never saw, and I'll never forget it, I looked through the entrance of that cemetery, all you saw was a sea of white crosses. It was something to behold. And right at sunset, right at dusk, and it was so touching, you know, and see all those crosses, one on top of the other, loads of them. And at that time of day, it was quite touching, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a time during the Battle of the Bulge you thought maybe the Germans were going to succeed with their plan?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, I don't think there was. Although we retreated at the time. And I wasn't anywhere near Bastogne, where they really got nailed or got encircled. And we were on the outside perimeter of that. So we were not involved in that at all. But we were, we did back off and, of course, regrouped and went forward again. But no, it was a scary thing when you realized these paratroopers had gotten down and they were infiltrating. You didn't know who you were dealing with or where they were at or anything like that. Just kind of creepy. END OF CD ONE, BEGIN CD TWO

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Because you knew that they were around. And it's so long ago, a lot of stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you encounter -- were the paratroopers, some of them were also infiltrating with American uniforms, weren't they? Is that right?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: For the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You encountered --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: They were in white. Yeah, it was snowy. It was cold, boy, it was ice cold. And we'd always, of course, try to not stay outside. We always tried a building or something that we could get into. Even if it meant a house, we moved the people into another part of the house and at least get in where it was warm. And then we used to, oh, we'd go hunting. And the first time I noticed, we were on the road and I saw this string of animals running up over a hill. I thought, boy, look at those dogs. They weren't dogs, they were deer, a whole string of them, just running in a line, you know. And the deer over there are a little smaller than our deer here. And we would go hunting for deer. And then if we'd get one, we'd turn it over to the -- skin it and turn it over to the kitchen. We had a couple of guys with us who from the west and they were quite the hunters. And we'd get a deer and then they'd skin it and bleed it and give the meat to the kitchen and we'd have venison. But you used to see them, used to see quite a few herds of them, running across the countryside, displaced by the gunfire and that sort of thing. And then one attack that we had, and I can't remember where it was or what it was, we were told about it, that it was going to happen, that they were going to light the front up with aircraft lights shining toward the German lines, to blind them, and use a frontal attack, in view of those lights they couldn't see what we were doing. And they did it. And the whole skyline was lit up with aircraft lights.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really, really bright floodlights.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Bright, very bright, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they mounted, or were they just stationary, or were they mounted on a tank?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, they were stationary. They were mounted on, mounted on railcars or trucks or whatever. But I know they tried this as a, just as an experiment, I guess, and used it for a frontal attack and just to blind the German troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I heard a guy talk about something, maybe the same thing, called Operation Gizmo; does that sound right?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It might have been a similar thing that he had.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: It might have been.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did it work?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: I guess it did. I never heard any more about it. We never did any more either. So whether it worked or not, I don't know. And then we had an occasion where, and it was icy, I come down a road and, unfortunately, my truck skidded on the ice and I hit a GI. And I felt so bad about it, and I stopped and went back, because I knocked him down. And I didn't know how badly he was hurt. And the troops that were with him told me: Go on, get out of here, get out of here. Because we were right on a road that was in open country and open to enemy fire, and they told me get the hell out of there with that truck. And so I did. But the next day I guess it was -- anyway, we slept in a barn, there was a dead German laying in the haymow where we slept. And we had our gun mounted outside this barn, or house, on the hillside where we could look across the valley. And that night I was on guard and I saw this fellow shuffling up the road. He didn't look -- he looked strange to me. Dark as pitch. I yelled, "Hande hoch," which was the term for "hands up," and I heard this garbled German. Here, it was a German soldier. I don't know whether he'd wandered away from his lines or what, but anyway he was wandering up the road and he came over to me. And fortunately, I didn't shoot, I didn't shoot at him. I could have, but I didn't. And all of a sudden a whole mob of GIs came out of the house and got him, took him prisoner, and they were interrogating him the last time I saw him. But that next day, we could see the tanks, German tanks, moving around in the woods across the valley from where we were at. And of course, we put our 57-millimeter in place. And they were telling us to "Fire it, fire it." Well, they pulled the firing pin and pulled it, and it didn't fire. And here, what had happened -- then they pulled the tank in alongside of it, so they fired it -- but what had happened, and we didn't realize it, I never thought of it I guess, but when we came off the ship and pulled that tank through the saltwater, the tank was buried in water. Why, we'd never taken the gun apart and cleaned it. And the salt had frozen the firing pin so that the firing pin would not work. It just, oomph, that's all you heard. It didn't fire the shell at all. Then they pulled the tank in, of course, and fired. And I don't know whether they hit the tank over on the other side of the valley or not. But we didn't realize that that damn pin was frozen solid in that gun. And here we're on outpost with a gun that wasn't working. It was soon after that they, the next stop we made, they pulled the thing down and spread a blanket on the ground and tore that down and cleaned it all out and got it working. But one of those things, you know, you never thought of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much -- do you remember anything about mail call, getting any letters from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. We'd have mail call pretty near every day, I guess. I don't know whether I got any -- whether I saved any of them upstairs. I've got a trunk upstairs where I got a -- I sent a German, what amounted to our M1, home. And a 9-millimeter Mauser, I got upstairs, sniper's rifle, that I got upstairs. And my dad cut the stock down and made a sporting stock out of it. Had a scope on it and everything. Put the target right on the point of the barrel, I'll tell you. And I haven't used it. I thought maybe I'd go hunting with it here, but I've never gotten the real ambition to go deer hunting here with it. But it's upstairs in the attic. And then I had a, when I ran into this tank with these German soldiers supporting it, I flopped down on the ground and covered myself up with a raincoat, and just played dead, because I wasn't about to attack eight people with rifles. And when they went by, I lifted the raincoat up and here was a P38 -- I've got that upstairs, too -- that they'd thrown down. And so I made a holster for that at some leather factory we got into over there. And while we were there, I had time enough to make a holster for it, and so I got it upstairs in a trunk. And then I picked up, and I don't know where I got it, but I know I stuck it in my bag and carried it with me, a German dagger. It's a saber, about that long, with a swastika and everything on it. I don't know who it belonged to or where, but I got it in one of the houses we were in and stuck it in my bag and kept it. It's probably got numbers on it. You could trace the numbers back and if they kept any records, you probably could find out who it belonged to, but I have no idea who it did belong to. But it was about that long. And of course, the two rifles. I had, when we were in Czechoslovakia, when we met up with the Russians, there was a farmer there, and I had all this stuff gathered together, rifles, and I forget what else was in that package -- oh, a great big German swastika flag. My wife's cousin had told her to ask me to send him the biggest swastika flag that I could find. Well, I found one. It was bigger than the ones that Perkins flies on top of their flagpoles now. It was a huge thing. Big swastika right in the middle. And I wrapped everything in that, rifles and all, broke them all down, and tagged them. And I didn't know whether they'd ever get home. But the way this farmer sewed that stuff up in burlap sacks, I mean he sewed it, hand-stitched it tight. Anybody had torn it apart, never got it back together again. And lo and behold, it all got home, every bit of it. I had a small white tag on it listing what was in the thing. And I had my doubts whether the firearms would get home. But by gosh, they did, every one of them. And so I didn't find this out until after I got back home. And my wife's cousin lived in Philadelphia. And his father and sisters told me that when he and his buddies got ahold of that German swastika flag, why, here, they flew it atop of the flagpole in their backyard in Germantown Philadelphia and had the cops all out after them. This was before the war was over. So I don't know whatever happened to the flag. I imagine they threw it away or burned it or something. But yeah, I said, "What? I can't believe that." Yeah, just as a prank, they put it up the top of their flagpole in his backyard. But, oh me, I don't know what else I could think of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any entertainment, get any shows, USO shows?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we saw some real good shows. Bob Hope was there. I think we saw -- I don't remember whether we saw Bob Hope. But one of the female singers -- I can't remember her name now either.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Frances Langford?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Frances Langford, yeah. Yeah, they had us, yeah, they brought those shows right up to the front line. And the other people that I give a lot of credit to were the Red Cross doughnut girls who'd bring the doughnuts and coffee up to the front lines. Had the doughnut wagons. And they'd hand us out shaving stuff, you know, simple things that we would enjoy and need. But they were right up there on the front lines, too. The big shows, saw quite a few of those. And those people really did a bang-up job. The USO brought them up and they did a great job. And of course, after the war and the shows that Bob Hope put on, we never saw him, but after the war in other war areas, he did a bang-up job for the GIs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, my -- the other, one of the other truckdrivers, name was Bill Jones, he lived in -- in fact, going over, he told me, he said, you know, he said, "I feel that I'm not going to come back from here." This was before we were even off the troop ship, before we even landed in Liverpool. And it wasn't too long after we went ashore, they were on a gun emplacement and he was killed. And I'll never forget that, because that's what he told me, he said, "You know," he said, "I don't think I'm going to come back from this." And he didn't. He didn't. And then the one time, like I said, the one time we stopped in the square of a town, I don't remember why they were taking the gun off the truck, or what, but they landed a shell right between the truck and the gun and got the whole damn crew all at once.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back to the States?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, my wife, we were married in Texas, during the war, in Texas City. And when I come back -- my wife came up here and stayed with my parents, because I had written her that I was on my way home. And it seemed like forever and a day getting out of those camps, getting processed through to get home. It was quite a joyful reunion. We landed at Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania, and from there we were given immediate, almost immediate, passes to come home right away. And I buddied up with somebody, and I forget, I don't remember who they were either now anymore, and we both left, came home -- they were from Ohio -- and both he and I drove back. I still had my car. It had been laid up all the time I was away. It was a '41 Plymouth coupe and almost brand new. And so I drove back to Indiantown Gap. And of course, I met my wife at the Pennsylvania station at 55th and Euclid there. When I came in, I came in on Pennsylvania. And it was quite gratifying getting home, I'll tell you. And I didn't see the Lady in the Harbor going away, but I sure saw her coming back. And I'll never forget that. The crowds that were lining the bridges as we came up under the Washington Bridge in New York, man, there were crowds on those bridges. And the biggest thing the GIs wanted when they got off that boat was a quart of milk. And they had the milk trucks right there on the dock with cases of milk. And you couldn't get enough of it. Couldn't get enough of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. Any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, not that I can really think of at the moment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Covered it as best as we could?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: I think so. Some of the more unusual things. I thought the most unusual is meeting that farmer that said he had a furniture store here in Cleveland. That was something else again I couldn't get over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he apparently had gone back to Germany and just got --

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: He'd gotten back to Germany, I guess, and apparently gotten stuck there and couldn't get out. There were a lot of people over there like that. And the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard of guys getting stuck and ending up in the military, but he ended up as a farmer.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, he was -- he couldn't speak that good of English either. But he knew enough when I said I was from Cleveland, he knew what Cleveland was. And I was taken aback when he said that, you know. But this world is a small place when you come right down to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, all right, you think we have it? Covered it?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, I hope I was able to tell you stuff you hadn't heard before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I mean, from the beginning, I never talked to anybody that did shore patrol in the gulf.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, we were assigned there as a -- well, we were an infantry unit, a battalion, that landed at Texas City, out of Camp Shelby, Mississippi. And we were there quite a while, a lot longer than I ever thought we would be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any fear that perhaps saboteurs were going to come ashore along the beaches?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yes, yes, that was the big thing. Because they had, in Texas City at the time, they had the only operating tin smelter in the world. And that's what we were down there for was for the refineries and because of that tin smelter. And we were there quite a while, longer than I would have ever thought we would have been. In fact, we got kind of spoiled, because we had almost had an open camp. And being an enlisted man, getting married, I lived illegally off base. We rented a place just, oh, a couple streets over from the camp, dump of a place, but I went home every night. Pass or no pass I could go home every night. But when we moved from Camp Shelby into Texas, an entirely different world. Texas was a dump -- or Mississippi was a dump. Camp Shelby was a horrible place. I didn't like that there at all. Then we went into Texas, it was an entirely different world. We got fed decently, the food was good. It was as different as night is from day going from Mississippi to Texas. And of course, Texas City, when we got there, Texas down in that area is so flat you can stand in a chair and see two years ahead, the way they put it. And the first place we hit was a place called the Club Cafe, right in the middle of what was one street of Texas City, a typical Texas town, and we had -- well, we were almost all from Ohio, and so Texas City had a lot of Ohio connections. A few other guys got married down there, too. Because my mother- and father-in-law wound up down there and he worked for Pan American Refineries. And my mother-in-law worked for the Monsanto Chemical Company. And I don't know whether you're old enough to recall the boat/ship that blew up in the channel down in Texas City?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: The Grandcamp. They pulled in there and they had ammonium nitrate fertilizer --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, I think I do remember that, yes.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: -- on board, in the hold, and somehow or other the ship caught fire. And the sudden change of temperature blew that hold of ammonium nitrate up. And my mother-in-law worked in the office for Monsanto that was right next to that dock. And when that blew, she was at work, it blew the whole wall out along where she worked, and they found her wandering around up in town after it was over with. Fortunately, she did not get hurt. But I had a couple of friends that were blown off the top of that tower, that they showed on the front page of the paper, and they wound up out in the gulf and a ship picked them up. But it was -- it may -- we were down there about two, three days after it happened. We got word that my mother-in-law had been involved in it and they couldn't find her. My father-in-law was going crazy looking for her. And they found her over in a hospital in Galveston, John Sealy Hospital in Galveston Island. And boy, that town was -- I mean it looked like a bomb area that I had seen overseas, I'll tell you. They found the drive shaft of that thing clear out the other side of town. But ever since then they have banned off-loading fertilizer on the docks down there. They don't do it anymore. They off-load it out at sea and bring it in. But that was quite an explosion. And then my wife worked for Monsanto for a while during the war while she was down there. And of course, one of my furloughs I didn't even bother coming home, I just stayed down there and worked for, I forget, for the railroad for a short time that I was on furlough, just to use up time really. But -- and then we went up to Camp Hood for a while. And that was a -- Camp Hood was, then, was up in the hills of Texas. And we weren't there too long though before we were shipped out and up to New York. And we weren't in New York too long. But everything, of course, then, was top secret. And of course, down in Galveston, anywhere along the coast down there, you didn't drive with headlights on the cars. You only used, well, parking lights at the most or no lights at all. And of course, all the army vehicles had the little blackout lights on them, had little slots in them, you could hardly see them. And you wouldn't have known when I came home on furlough from Texas City, you wouldn't -- it was like two different countries. You'd come up here, you'd never know there was a war going on. Down there everything was black, black, black. Everything. And of course, we were stationed then out on the end of the island at Fort San Jacinto, which was a permanent military shore gun emplacement. And we started to move the ammunition out of there. These were the big 16-inch guns. And we started to move the ammunition out of there into railroad cars. I don't know where they were going to ship it to. And then during one of the hurricanes down there, I never saw the army move so fast in my life. We were having lunch and all of a sudden they come in and say: Get ready to move, there's a hurricane coming in. And man, they moved us up into Fort Crockett, into permanent barracks, so fast it would make your head swim. And we rode the hurricane out on the island there. But we couldn't get off the island for over a week. The backwaters had all come in and flooded out the roads, and we just couldn't get back into the mainland at all. But Texas was a good state to be in. We got fed. And I liked Texas. I really did. And we've been down there. Of course, my mother- and father-in-law lived down there before he died and before my mother moved up here -- my mother-in-law moved up here. It was an entirely different world. And Texans were good people to get along with. And we've made trips down there since and went out into the Rio Grande Valley and up to Sanderson, which is out in the middle of the desert, hot, plenty hot, Del Rio. And of course, my wife went to school down there in Texas City.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. My dad went to Texas, too.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Did he?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Gainesville. Closer to Oklahoma, I guess, north of Dallas.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, that would be more toward, that would be more toward Camp Hood. Temple. Well, Camp Hood was at Temple.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This was Camp Howze in Gainesville.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think he also went through Shelby for a little while.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Did he go through Shelby?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think so. I have the list of camps that I have for him and I think that was one of them.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, well, I know what he went through when he went through Shelby. I hated that camp. Oh, lord, that was a big, big installation though, too. And of course, that's where we first landed. And they split us up down there when the war started. And I didn't drive a truck when I first went in. I was in the C Company, I think it was, the 166th Infantry Regiment, but part of the old 42nd Rainbow Division. And a friend of mine was in the service company and driving trucks. And so I got the hell out of the infantry company so I didn't have to walk, and got into service company and drove a truck after that. And of course, when we were transferred into the 90th Division, I wasn't driving the big trucks. I first had a 2-1/2 ton cargo truck and then, when we left, joined the 90th Division, I was assigned to a low silhouette Dodge 6 by 6 that we towed the antitank gun with, 57-millimeter antitank gun. And that, of course, I towed that all through Europe. And I got into a, one of the towns that we got into in France, we went into it not knowing that there were no more enemy forces in the town. And we went on in on a main road, head on, into it. And I'll tell you, you didn't know whether you were going to get shot at or not. I drove standing up in the seat of the truck, truck in gear, and just standing up there wheeling the thing ready to dive for the ditch. And when we got into the town that night, we had a fellow that was of French extraction that was part of our gun crew. And he'd gone nosing around after we got into the town and got settled. And he come and he said, "Hey," he said, "I found a Free French headquarters," FFE headquarters. He said, "Come on, let's go have a drink with them." I said, "Okay." So we found them. I don't know whereabouts in the town we were at, but anyway, we found them. And you never saw such a bunch of rough renegades in all your life. You'd look at them and damned if you were going to turn your back on them. But they were the Free French guys who kicked the Germans out of town. They were part of that Free French outfit that were the underground fighting group of the Frenchmen. And oh, they were rough. One arm, one leg, one eye, patches over the eye. And you'd go in there and they'd look at you, you know, and your hair would go up on the back of your head. But they were the friendly bunch that did the job of kicking the -- they kicked the Germans out of town and they got all the prostitutes and walked them up and down the streets without any clothes on. They were rougher than hell. They were really rough. And they looked it. They looked it. But they, as much as people don't like to believe it, we owe them a lot, because they did a lot of clearing of towns. When they knew that the Americans were coming and were just about to occupy those towns, they were the ones that did the underground work and kicked the Germans out and made sure they weren't there. And knocked them away from their guns and that sort of thing. Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think we got it.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: -- I guess that's about all you can jog my memory from me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think you covered a lot. You did very good.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Probably a lot of this you've heard before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, not -- you know, some of it I have. You know, I've talked to a lot of guys that went through the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, that was quite extensive, that was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah, it was so extensive that you do find a lot of guys.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. And of course, we were on the perimeter of that. We didn't get surrounded or pinned down like the guys in Bastogne did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think that's what Gordon said, he was kind of a -- he wasn't really in the middle of it.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: No, we were -- when that happened, I know we were down in the Saar River, and all of a sudden they said, "Get ready to move out." But I'll tell you, that damned English Channel, I'll never forget the day we were put off on that barge. I'll never forget the feeling I had with the weather the way it was. Weather just like today, just exactly like today, gray and miserable, misty, rain. I think we had one German aircraft that flew across the beach that morning as we were going ashore.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Boy, he got an eyeful, didn't he?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yeah, he sure did. I don't think he was firing his guns as he went either.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: He'd have been a little bit stupid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Then I was in another place in Europe, on the mainland, when we had bedded down and got the gun in place, and I was going across a field, and all of a sudden here comes them Messerschmitts, over the top of the hill and down the valley. He was just hedgehopping. And I don't know whether he was firing guns or not. It looked like I could see them. But man, you never such an ugly swirling prop coming at you in your life. And you'd dive for the ground and hope to hell they'd miss you.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: You ate a lot of mud over there, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Yes, I did. I told my dad when I come home, he was quite an outdoor sportsman, and he'd like to take the car and go as far as he could and then take the canoe off the top of the car and backpack into wherever he went, and I said, "Well," I said, "I'll go fishing, I'll go hunting with you, but, you damn sure better have a nice warm cabin at the end of it, because I am not going to sleep out in the dirt and water again." I said, "I've I slept in enough mud holes."

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: And you know, his father was, as he said, quite a hunter. But he used to go, just like by walking or horseback riding, out to Oregon territory, so I mean this sleeping on the ground and all this stuff was just as normal to him as getting into a bed and going to sleep. He just couldn't understand why Fred just didn't want to go. And my dearest girlfriend's daughter is married to a man who is just like my father-in-law. And I told him, I says, "Tom," I said, "when you've had four years of that and all the body parts you see laying around aren't animal," I said, "you just get a stomach full of it and it's no longer your cup of tea." But he's a pretty good fisherman though. Put him in a boat and he's happy.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: But when I came home I said no more, no more of that, no more. When you stopped, that was the first thing you looked for was a shovel to start digging a hole for yourself, and hope to hell that you didn't get into a woods where you got a lot of shell bursts. And I lost two trucks. One of them they put a mortar shell right down between the driver's -- the passenger seat and the dashboard, burnt that up. And then the other one I got into, I forget where we were going, I got into an accident and smashed one up. But the one that got burned up, we were on the side of a hill and they lobbed a mortar shell into it and caught it on fire. Of course, we had high-explosive shells on board, in the back of it. And we never really used the high-explosive shells though. In fact, the one time we tried to fire the damn gun, the pin was frozen in it and it wouldn't fire. And we didn't even know it. And here, we'd been on outposts, and fortunately we never got attacked. And, of course, just lucky we had, at that time, that we had a tank close by and he let loose. And I don't know whether he hit what he was firing at or not. (Interview resumed as follows:)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Part 2 on January 14, 2005. So go ahead.

sp.speaker: Frederick B. Wolfe
sp.p: Well, this is going to be some of the stuff I forgot in the first part of it. After the war was over, we were stationed in a town called Grafenwohr. It was about, I believe, about 10 miles from Weiden, which was the 90th Division headquarters at the time, temporary headquarters, set up in Weiden. And we used to travel between Grafenwohr and Weiden. And this German military tank, armored camp that we were stationed at on occupation duty, was the site of a German armored division. And I don't know whether I told this in the first part or not, but on this camp there was a lot of miniature training tanks, one-man training tanks. And of course, anything that was motorized, the GIs got ahold of, motorcycles, training tanks, they'd run the hell out of them. And they ran these things around the place until they drove the drive shafts out of them. They were still operable, and they just had a lot of fun with them. But anyway, in this camp, Grafenwohr was surrounded with woods, heavy woods. And when the bombers came in, they bombed the hell out of this place. And they must have had the woods earmarked on their charts, because they completely surrounded the area with bombs and they never put a bomb in the woods where the gas shells were at. And these woods were hiding stockpiles of poison gas shells, which I don't think a lot of people realized that the Germans had, and they had plenty of it, phosgene and mustard gas, piled in, oh, stacks 10 feet high or higher in wicker baskets. And all marked. And while we were there we had an incident where some kids got in there -- and they had them stacked so there were fire breaks between the piles -- but we had some kids got in there and started a fire. And they evacuated Grafenwohr for a temporary time until they got it out. But it was a touchy situation at the time. And every house, I don't know whether these were officers quarters or -- they had to be army personnel quarters because they were on the base -- but every one of these houses had a sealed rubber-gasketed room in the basement that filtered the air -- and obviously, because they were around this gas dump -- in case they had an accident I would imagine. But they demolished the buildings and we found, in the basements, were these sealed-off, gasketed rooms, apparently that were airtight and would filter air, probably for a safety precaution is all I can imagine they might have been for. And of course, they were all a part of the grounds surrounding the camp. And we used to travel between Grafenwohr and Weiden quite frequently on a dirt road, it wasn't an improved road. And then there was another occasion, as we were coming up through Germany, I don't know whether this was in the first tape or not, where -- and I don't know the name of the town -- where we had gone into the town under white flags. They had stretched white flags from the windows of the buildings in the town. And as we were going in, we were fired on. And they backed off and threw artillery in on that town and blew it to hell, they burned it down. That town was nothing but a sea of fire after that happened. So that was the consequence of that. But they had gas shells and they had lots of it, lots of it. They never got a chance to use it apparently, or didn't use it. But they had it in -- there were fire breaks down between these tall piles of shells. And it was an eerie situation to drive down through the woods through these things. But that was about the only incidence that I can remember after the war. And I think that's about the sum total of what I missed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. END OF CD TWO
